opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the places where the current conversation about AI goes a bit off the rails. There's this tendency to think of knowledge as something that lives in a single head, or now in a single model, as if you could just pour all the facts into one container and then you'd have intelligence. But that's not how knowledge has ever really worked for humans.

Knowledge is a collective phenomenon. It lives in communities, in practices, in institutions, in the ways people talk to each other and argue with each other and trust each other or don't. Think about medicine. No single doctor knows medicine. There's a whole system of training, of apprenticeship, of journals, of hospitals, of norms about what counts as evidence, and of people checking each other's work. That system is the thing that holds the knowledge, and culture is the glue that makes it function over generations.

And the renewal part is crucial. Knowledge isn't static. It decays if it isn't used, and it gets stale if it isn't challenged. Culture provides the mechanisms by which young people come in, learn the existing ways of doing things, and then push back on them. That tension between tradition and novelty is where a lot of progress comes from. Economists have thought about this, anthropologists have thought about this, and I think computer scientists have been a bit naive about it.

So when I look at large language models, I see them as a kind of cultural artifact. They're a compression of a lot of what humans have written down, and that's genuinely useful. But they're downstream of culture; they don't by themselves renew it. If we start replacing the human processes that generate new knowledge, the arguing, the experimenting, the local expertise, with systems that just recycle what's already been said, we risk a kind of slow erosion.

What I'd like to see instead is that we think about these technologies as participants in a larger system, a market or an ecosystem, if you will, where they help connect people, help surface knowledge that's distributed and local, and create new kinds of collaboration. Done well, that could actually strengthen culture's role in maintaining and renewing knowledge. Done poorly, it hollows it out. And that's really an engineering and design choice, one that involves economics and social science as much as it involves machine learning.

r001.rationale: It says knowledge decays if it is not used, but does not say that decay happens rapidly.

r002.rationale: It identifies institutions and the broader system of training, journals, hospitals, and shared norms as holding knowledge and functioning over generations.

r003.rationale: It describes new knowledge emerging through local expertise, experimentation, argument, and collaboration within a larger system.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't think of knowledge as something that lives in individual heads, or in individual machines for that matter. It lives in collectives. It lives in the interactions among people, in institutions, in practices that get handed down and modified over time. And culture is the name we give to that whole apparatus.

If you look at science as an example, the knowledge isn't the paper. The paper is a kind of artifact. The knowledge is in a community that knows how to read the paper, knows what to be skeptical about, knows which results tend to replicate and which don't, knows the tacit stuff that never gets written down. A graduate student learns most of what matters not from textbooks but from sitting in a lab, watching how senior people argue, seeing what questions they take seriously. That's cultural transmission. And it's not just preservation, it's renewal, because every generation reinterprets what it inherits. The things that were central become background and new questions move to the center.

I think this matters enormously for how we think about AI, because there's a tendency right now to imagine intelligence as this monolithic thing, a single system that knows everything and reasons about everything. And I've been a bit of a contrarian on this. I think the more interesting and more realistic picture is a collective one. Markets are collective intelligence. Scientific communities are collective intelligence. Language itself is a kind of distributed knowledge system that no individual created and no individual fully understands. The intelligence is in the system, in the flows of information and incentives among many agents, human and now increasingly computational.

And what culture does in that picture is provide the error-correction. It's the mechanism by which a collective notices when something it believed is wrong and updates. Peer review, debate, tradition, even things like humor and storytelling, these are all ways a society keeps its knowledge from decaying or calcifying. If you remove the humans from that loop, if you just have machines trained on a snapshot of human text, you've frozen the culture at a moment in time. You've got the artifacts without the living process that produced them and keeps correcting them.

So when people ask me whether large models "know" things, I tend to say the question is a little off. They've absorbed a lot of cultural artifacts. Whether that counts as knowledge depends on whether they're embedded in a system that can renew it, that can be wrong and find out it's wrong. That's the part I care about, and I think it's where the real engineering and social design challenges are. Not building a smarter individual, but building better collectives, and being thoughtful about how these new tools plug into the cultural processes that have been maintaining human knowledge for a very long time.

r001.rationale: It says culture keeps knowledge from decaying, but does not state that knowledge decays rapidly.

r002.rationale: It identifies institutions and scientific communities as places where knowledge is transmitted, preserved, and renewed over generations.

r003.rationale: It describes collective interactions and generational reinterpretation, but does not clearly say new knowledge emerges through bottom-up activity.

astra-6.text:
I think culture is part of how we know things, not just a backdrop to knowledge. An individual can understand a small piece of the world, but most of what we rely on is distributed across other people, practices, and institutions. We learn whom to ask, what counts as a good explanation, and when to question an answer. Those are things we acquire culturally.

And a lot of knowledge lives in practice. You work alongside somebody and discover how they formulate a problem, which details they pay attention to, when they say, “That doesn’t look right.” It’s difficult to capture all of that in a textbook. Maintaining knowledge means maintaining the settings in which people can develop that judgment.

But there’s a tension, because the same practices that preserve understanding can become habits that prevent you from seeing something new. So renewal requires room for disagreement, for people coming from different backgrounds to ask questions that seem strange at first. You need continuity, but you also need the ability to revise what gets passed along.

That makes knowledge a collective achievement. The question isn’t only whether we have smart individuals. It’s whether we have ways of working together that allow us to preserve what we’ve learned and discover where it stops being useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses maintaining and renewing knowledge but does not say knowledge decays rapidly.

r002.rationale: It mentions institutions as places where knowledge is distributed, but does not clearly identify organizations as a means of preserving knowledge over time.

r003.rationale: It describes learning through practice and collaboration, but does not state that new knowledge emerges through bottom-up activity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think culture is part of how knowledge lives. We tend to imagine knowledge as something you can write down—a theorem, a set of facts, an algorithm. But knowing also involves judgment: which questions matter, when an abstraction is useful, when it’s misleading. A great deal of that gets passed on through working together, through examples, through criticism.

Think about an apprenticeship. You’re learning techniques, but you’re also learning what to pay attention to. You watch someone get stuck, change their mind, recognize that a result is surprising. A textbook has a hard time conveying all of that.

And there’s a tension here, because the practices that preserve knowledge can also become practices that protect authority. A healthy intellectual culture needs continuity, but it also needs ways for newcomers to say, “Why are we doing it this way?” and have that question taken seriously. So maintaining knowledge and renewing it are closely connected. You preserve the capacity to understand and inquire, and that includes the capacity to revise what you’ve inherited.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preserving and renewing knowledge but does not state that knowledge decays rapidly.

r002.rationale: It describes intellectual culture and working together, but does not identify organizations as a means of preserving knowledge over time.

r003.rationale: It says newcomers can question inherited practices, but does not describe new knowledge as emerging through bottom-up activity.
